text:
A: Hi. Er, hello.
B: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
A: Andrew. Sorry, Prajakta, is that right?
B: Yes. First time. That's rare.
A: I was concentrating.
B: So what do you do?
A: Erm, mapping. GIS, for a water company. Pipe networks, flood risk, that sort of thing. I'm in Beeston, just outside Nottingham.
B: Is that why there's a map behind you?
A: Sort of. That's an old Ordnance Survey one, about 1900. The old ones are more of a hobby, really. You can see where the pits were, and the railways that aren't there any more.
B: And the clothes on the radiator?
A: Er. That's a cycling jersey. I went out this morning and got rained on. I should've moved it before the call, I suppose.
B: I noticed it on the photo earlier. It's fine.
A: It's honest, at least. What about you?
B: QC analyst. Pharmaceutical manufacturing, in Stevenage. I test the batches before they're released.
A: So, checking things are what they say they are.
B: Yes. And checking other people haven't made mistakes.
A: That's quite a lot of my job as well, actually. Contractors send in survey data and half of it's wrong. Pipe diameters in the depth column, or the coordinates put a manhole in the middle of the Trent. And I'm the one who's meant to work out what they actually meant.
B: Do you tell them?
A: Er, mostly I just fix it. Then I send a polite email.
B: I tell them. Directly. People think I'm sharp because of it, but if I don't say anything, it happens again next week.
A: You're probably right. I should be more like that.
B: Probably.
A: Erm. Are those spice tins on the shelf? The steel ones?
B: Yes. Do you cook?
A: Most nights, yeah. Dal, a chickpea curry, a few things from a Middle Eastern cookbook I'm working through. Nothing fancy.
B: Where do you buy your spices?
A: Er, the supermarket, mostly.
B: That's the problem. They sit on the shelf for a year and they taste of nothing. Go to an Indian grocer. Buy whole spices, small packets, and toast them yourself. I drive to Hitchin for mine.
A: Right. There's a few in Nottingham. I'll try that.
B: You'll notice the difference. Straight away.
A: I'll report back. Well, I won't, I suppose. But I'll know.
B: Yes. You'll know.
A: Do you get back to India much?
B: Every year or so. Pune. Usually December, for three weeks. I hate the flight, and leaving is worse. My father had a heart problem two years ago, so each time I go I'm thinking, is this the last time I see him like this.
A: Yeah. My dad had a scare last year. It's not the same, he's only up the road, but I get it. You sort of watch them differently after.
B: Yes. That's exactly it. You watch them.
A: Is he alright now?
B: He's fine. He walks every morning. My mother phones me if he doesn't.
A: That's good. Mine's back up ladders, which is less good.
B: Then tell him. Directly.
A: Ha. Yeah, maybe I'll start with him.
B: Where would you go? If you could travel anywhere.
A: Er, Iceland, I think. Or Japan. Somewhere I could—
